content: CD16, also referred to as FcγRIII, is a differentiation molecule present on the surface of natural killer (NK) cells, neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages. It is classified into two forms: FcγRIIIa (CD16a) and FcγRIIIb (CD16b), both of which are involved in signal transduction. CD16 is a key membrane receptor in NK cell-mediated lysis and is part of the immunoglobulin superfamily (IgSF), playing a critical role in antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). This molecule is also utilized in isolating specific immune cell populations through techniques like fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) or magnetic-activated cell sorting, using antibodies targeting CD16. CD16 is a type III Fcγ receptor and exists in two forms in humans: FcγRIIIa (CD16a) and FcγRIIIb (CD16b), which share 96% sequence similarity in their extracellular immunoglobulin-binding regions. FcγRIIIa is expressed as a transmembrane receptor on mast cells, macrophages, and NK cells, while FcγRIIIb is exclusively expressed on neutrophils. Notably, FcγRIIIb is the only Fc receptor anchored to the cell membrane via a glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI) linker and is involved in calcium mobilization and neutrophil degranulation. Together, FcγRIIIa and FcγRIIIb activate processes like degranulation, phagocytosis, and oxidative burst, enabling neutrophils to eliminate opsonized pathogens. These receptors bind to the Fc portion of IgG antibodies, triggering ADCC in human NK cells. CD16 is essential for ADCC processes mediated by human monocytes. Monocytes expressing CD16 exhibit diverse ADCC capabilities in the presence of specific antibodies, allowing them to kill primary leukemic cells, cancer cell lines, and hepatitis B virus-infected cells. Additionally, CD16 can mediate the direct killing of certain virally infected and cancer cells without the need for antibodies. Upon binding to ligands like the conserved region of IgG antibodies, CD16 on NK cells induces the transcription of genes encoding surface activation molecules (e.g., IL-2R/CD25) and inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ and TNF). This cytokine mRNA expression is regulated by the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFATp), a cyclosporin A-sensitive factor, through a calcium-dependent mechanism. The crystal structures of FcεRIα, FcγRIIa, FcγRIIb, and FcγRIII have been experimentally determined, revealing a conserved immunoglobulin-like structure. A common feature among all Ig superfamily Fc receptors is the acute hinge angle between the Nand C-terminal Ig domains. Specifically, the structure of CD16 (FcγRIIIb) consists of two immunoglobulin-like domains with an interdomain hinge angle of approximately 50°. The Fc-binding region of the receptor carries a net positive charge, complementing the negatively charged receptor-binding regions on Fc. CD16 plays a pivotal role in the early activation of NK cells following vaccination. Downregulation of CD16 can moderate NK cell responses and maintain immune homeostasis in T celland antibody-dependent signaling pathways. In healthy individuals, cross-linking of CD16 by immune complexes induces ADCC in NK cells. This pathway can also be exploited in immunotherapy to target cancerous or diseased cells. For instance, after influenza vaccination, CD16 downregulation is associated with increased influenza-specific plasma antibodies and correlates with NK cell degranulation. CD16 is frequently used as a marker to identify subsets of human immune cells. While markers like CD11b and CD33 are traditionally used for myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), additional markers such as CD14 and CD15 are required to distinguish between neutrophils and monocytes. Neutrophils are CD14-low and CD15-high, whereas monocytes are CD14-high and CD15-low. CD16 further differentiates these cell types, as mature neutrophils are CD16-high, while eosinophils and monocytes are CD16-low. CD16 expression also varies across neutrophil developmental stages, with increasing expression observed in metamyelocytes, banded neutrophils, and mature neutrophils. CD16 is a potential target in cancer immunotherapy due to its expression on neutrophils. Margetuximab, an Fc-optimized monoclonal antibody targeting HER2 on tumor cells, preferentially binds to CD16a over CD16b. CD16 also plays a role in antibody-targeting cancer therapies. Bispecific antibody fragments, such as anti-CD19/CD16, enable the targeting of immunotherapeutic drugs to cancer cells. Anti-CD19/CD16 diabodies enhance NK cell responses to B-cell lymphomas. Additionally, targeting extrinsic factors like FasL or TRAIL to tumor cell surfaces activates death receptors, inducing apoptosis through autocrine and paracrine mechanisms.
